item.title: The limits of higher-order interactions in shaping chimera states
item.description: arXiv:2610.31997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In neuronal networks, chimera states, characterized by the coexistence of coherent and incoherent populations, have attracted considerable attention in the study of collective brain dynamics, due to its potential implications for neurological disorders such as epilepsy. Their emergence has been extensively investigated with a particular emphasis on the role of network topology, both in conventional pairwise interactions and, more recently, in higher-order interaction networks. Here, we propose a generalized framework for neuronal hypergraphs incorporating higher-order interactions through attractive chemical and repulsive electrical coupling. Using networks of FitzHugh--Nagumo neurons with interaction orders d=2,3,4, corresponding to (d+1)-body interactions within a framework that can be extended to higher d, we numerically investigate the emergence of chimera states under the combined effect of attractive and repulsive coupling and we compare the resulting dynamics with those of their corresponding clique-projected networks. Our results reveal that, both dynamical similarities and qualitative differences between genuine higher-order interactions on hypergraphs and their pairwise representations. While higher-order interactions often support broader chimera regions, we show that clique projections can also preserve or promote chimera states, even in regimes where the corresponding hypergraphs exhibit fully incoherent dynamics. Therefore, these findings suggest that chimera formation is not only influenced by the topology or by the interaction order but also by the form of the coupling functions and the balance between attractive and repulsive interactions, offering further insights into collective dynamics in neuronal networks.
item.dc:creator: Ediline L. F. Nguessap, Thierry Njougouo, Fernando Fagundes Ferreira

item.title: From Heterogeneity to Function: Enhanced Modular Dynamic Range in Hierarchical Brain Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.32328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hierarchical and modular organization defines brain architecture, yet how it supports flexible computation and functional specialization remains unclear. Although dynamic range is a hallmark of efficient information processing, its distribution across modules and hierarchical levels remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that hierarchical-modular networks naturally generate heterogeneous modular dynamics and firing rates, extending regimes of critical-like dynamics with enhanced intrinsic timescales, reflecting critical slowing down, and diverse scaling exponents without fine-tuning near criticality. Intrinsic timescales increase across hierarchical levels, while their dispersion within levels emerges only when connectivity profiles and firing rates are heterogeneous. We introduce modular dynamic range to quantify how individual modules respond to external inputs and show that heterogeneity enhances both global and module-specific sensitivity, with modular intrinsic timescales increasing with dynamic range. Local stimulation reduces dynamic range in homogeneous networks but enhances it in heterogeneous networks relative to global stimulation. Moreover, selectively stimulating intermediate hierarchical levels maximizes both global and modular dynamic range, revealing a principle of functional specialization. In heterogeneous networks, modular dynamic range is more variable and increases even in unstimulated modules, demonstrating distributed computational benefits beyond directly stimulated regions. Together, these findings establish heterogeneity as a mechanism through which hierarchical-modular networks sustain critical-like dynamics, generate hierarchical timescales, and distribute computational sensitivity, providing a basis for functional specialization without fine-tuning to criticality.
item.dc:creator: Filipe V. Torres, Mauro Copelli, Leonardo L. Gollo
